title: First communion
hook: a child's first time at the table, remembered for life

segments.voice: Yesterday, chrism: blessed oil, the same oil on different clocks. Your line was sealed.

A line of children walks up the aisle, two by two. Some girls in white dresses, a few with veils that keep slipping. Boys in shirts buttoned to the top, which they'll undo the second this is over. Grandparents twisting around in the pews with phones up. Each child has practiced this: hands held a certain way, the right answer to say. Then one small girl reaches the front, and it isn't practice anymore. A piece of bread the size of a coin, and a word spoken just to her. Years later she might not remember the homily. She'll probably remember the dress.
screen: `A LINE OF CHILDREN, TWO BY TWO.`
`A PIECE OF BREAD, THE SIZE OF A COIN.`

segments.voice: First communion means a child's first time receiving the bread, and in some churches the cup, at the Lord's table. When depends on the church. In Catholic parishes, a child is usually baptized as a baby and receives first communion later in childhood, after classes, often with a family celebration. The Orthodox do it differently. As yesterday showed, an Orthodox baby is baptized and anointed in one service, and can receive communion right away, a tiny spoonful of bread and wine. So a child raised Orthodox won't remember a first communion; there was never a time they weren't at the table. Protestant churches vary. Some wait until a child is confirmed, some until a child can say what the meal means, and some welcome any baptized child. Each way has a page it leans on. Those who wait often point to Paul: "let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup." Those who welcome the very young often point to Mark. People bring little children to Jesus, and the disciples tell them off. "But when Jesus saw it, he was much displeased, and said unto them, Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God." Underneath both, a psalm: "O taste and see that the LORD is good." Taste: a mouth, a piece of bread, a first time. Each of these churches is trying to do right by that taste, and they disagree, in earnest, about when.
screen: `A CHILD'S FIRST TIME AT THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Let one first time come back to you: a first communion if you had one, a first meal in a new home, the first time someone let you sit at the grown-ups' table. Go slowly: what you wore, who was near, what it tasted like. If you pray, thank God for the person who brought you to that table; if you don't, just thank them in your mind.
First communion. A child's first time at the Lord's table, which comes at different ages in different churches.
Your line: the first taste. O taste and see, the psalm says. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-five, done.

howItsDone: Catholic children usually receive first communion in childhood after a period of preparation, often in a parish celebration; Orthodox Christians receive from infancy; Protestant churches differ, some after confirmation, some when a child can understand, some at any age after baptism.

notes: Editor: cut the unsourced 'families plan for months'; 'nobody remembers' narrowed to a child raised Orthodox; dropped 'Not study, not agree with', which repeated day 1332's 'Not think about, not agree with'; original note corrected (1 Peter 2:3 has the indicative ἐγεύσασθε, not the imperative).

Catholic practice: first communion is typically received around the age of reason (about seven) after preparation; the script avoids the age under the claims rule and says 'later in childhood, after classes'. 'Families plan for months' and white dresses/veils are general description; confirm tone.
Orthodox infants receive communion by spoon (bread and wine together); confirm wording 'a tiny spoonful of bread and wine'.

Protestant variety described with 'some'; the pairing of 1 Corinthians 11:28 with those who wait and Mark 10:14 with those who welcome is a simplification of real arguments on both sides. Confirm fair to each.
'Each of these churches is trying to do right by that taste' is an interpretive line; confirm acceptable or soften.
